top_cited_works.title: Construction of Dynamic Multifidelity Locally Optimized Surrogate Models
top_cited_works.abstract: The conceptual design phase for the development of new and revolutionary aircraft should include both low- and high-fidelity multidisciplinary engineering analyses to enable reasonable computational cost and accuracy tradeoffs. Multifidelity locally optimized surrogate models can be employed to fuse the multifidelity information to give an accurate representation of the underlying design space. These surrogates can be further enhanced with derivative information and augmented with dynamic training point selection to reduce overall computational cost. In this paper, a framework for multifidelity locally optimized surrogate models is developed, and the superior accuracy for the same computational cost or cheaper cost for the same accuracy compared to standard single-fidelity global surrogate models is demonstrated via analytic test functions. The multifidelity locally optimized surrogate models are also applied to the creation of an aerodynamic database involving the steady turbulent flow around a NACA 00xx airfoil, where the influence of Mach number, angle of attack, and thickness-to-chord ratio variations on the lift and drag coefficient are studied.

top_cited_works.title: Design Optimization Utilizing Gradient/Hessian Enhanced Surrogate Model
top_cited_works.abstract: In this paper, gradient/Hessian-enhanced surrogate models have been developed based on Kriging approaches. The gradient/Hessian-enhanced Kriging methods have been developed based on direct and indirect formulations. The efficiencies of these methods are compared by analytical function fitting, aerodynamic data modeling and 2D airfoil drag minimization problems. For the aerodynamic problems, efficient CFD gradient/Hessian calculation methods are utilized that make use of adjoint and automatic differentiation techniques. The gradient/Hessian-enhanced surrogate models are shown to be useful in the development of efficient design optimization, aerodynamic database construction, and uncertainty analysis.

recent_works.title: Multi-Fidelity Kriging Surrogate Models Applied to the Second UQ Challenge Problem
recent_works.abstract: In this paper, a multi-fidelity kriging surrogate model is employed to tackle the second uncertainty quantification challenge problem where participants are asked to make an estimate of the predictive capability of XFOIL for lift, drag, and moment coefficients at four conditions given ``truth'' (RANS) data in seven different locations (one condition coincides with a truth data point, two are interpolatory, and one is extrapolatory). Accurate surrogate models, once obtained, can be employed for evaluating a large number of designs for uncertainty quantification, optimization, or design space exploration.

recent_works.title: Summary of the Second AIAA Uncertainty Quantification Challenge Problem for Aerodynamics
recent_works.abstract: In early 2025, the AIAA Fluid Dynamics Technical Committee Uncertainty Quantification Discussion Group announced its second community Challenge Problem. Similar to the first Challenge Problem in 2024, the second Challenge Problem tasks participants with applying methods in verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification towards the analysis of airfoil simulations using a common panel method code; however, unlike the first Challenge Problem, the second Challenge Problem emphasizes the quantification of model form uncertainty and the interpolation and/or extrapolation thereof. In this summary paper, a brief overview of the second Challenge Problem is presented. A short description of each method (provided by participants) used to solve the Challenge Problem is also included. The participant results are compared. Nine different teams using ten different approaches participated; overall the predictions are all fairly comparable, showing that the field has reached some level of maturity.

recent_works.title: Multi-Fidelity Gradient-based Approach to the Aerostructural Optimization Benchmark Problem
recent_works.abstract: This paper describes our approach and results for the benchmark model and optimization problem proposed by working group 1 for the special session on High-Fidelity Aeroelastic Design Optimization Applications and Benchmarks at the 2026 AIAA SciTech Forum. A gradient-based multi-fidelity constrained optimization approach is applied to this aeroelastic fuel burn minimization of a Boeing 717-like wing with a lift and a buffet constraint and utilizing three planform and one flow design variable (aspect ratio, sweep, taper and angle of attack). The highest and lowest fidelity levels considered are Euler and panel solutions, respectively, all combined with a modal structural solver. The coupling of the two solvers and adjoint gradient computations are accomplished with FUNtoFEM. The optimization results show that a 20% reduction in fuel burn is possible while producing enough lift for cruise without buffeting. The multi-fidelity approach outperforms the high-fidelity one in terms of both robustness and computational cost for most starting points considered.

recent_works.title: Comparison of Gradient-based and Global Autoencoded Lift-constrained Drag Minimizations
recent_works.abstract: In this paper a traditional gradient-based quasi-Newton BFGS Optimizer as well as a global optimizer are applied to lift-constrained drag minimizations for steady inviscid flow over a transonic NACA 0012 airfoil with six Hicks-Henne sine bump shape design variables. For the global optimization, an autoencoder is used to perform a design dimensionality reduction and a surrogate model is constructed in the reduced dimension which is then employed in the global optimization. Results show that both methods lead to successful optimizations at comparable computational costs.

recent_works.title: Impact of High Freestream Turbulence on Low-Pressure Turbine Endwall Flow—Part II: Endwall Flow Dynamics
recent_works.abstract: Abstract The flow field surrounding low-pressure turbine blades is associated with significant losses in the endwall region. The exact location and behavior of the endwall structures are tied to the incoming boundary layer state; therefore, the incoming freestream turbulence is expected to impact dynamic characteristics of these structures and the associated losses. As discussed in Part I, the incoming turbulence intensity was varied between <1% and 7% at three different Reynolds numbers within a linear cascade of high-lift high-work low-pressure turbine blades. The focus of this article will be on the effect elevated freestream turbulence has on the unsteady dynamics of the endwall flow structures. Three planes of high-speed stereoscopic particle image velocimetry were collected within the passage of the turbine blades capturing cross-sectional slices of key endwall vortices. From a detailed flow analysis completed with stereoscopic particle image velocimetry (SPIV) measurements, it was established that elevating the turbulence levels had a direct impact on the locations and time-dependent characteristics of the endwall topology.
